The wind howled like a banshee, rattling the glass of the lantern room. Elias, the keeper of the St. Jude Light, watched the grey Atlantic churn below. It was a lonely life, but the solitude suited him.

At low tide the next morning, Elias walked the rocky shore to inspect the foundation. Among the kelp and driftwood, a flash of green caught his eye. It was a wine bottle, corked tight and heavy with sand.

Back in the warmth of his cottage, Elias pried the cork free. Inside was a rolled piece of parchment, brittle with age. He unrolled it carefully. The handwriting was elegant, looping script.

*“To the Keeper of the Light,”* it read. *“I am writing this on the eve of my departure, 1892. I leave behind a chest of gold buried beneath the third stone of the eastern wall. But I leave a warning: the sea is hungry. Do not take what is not yours, lest the tide take you in return.”*

Elias’s heart hammered. He grabbed a lantern and a crowbar and rushed to the eastern wall. He counted three stones from the corner and pried the heavy granite loose. Beneath it lay a small, iron-bound chest.

He lifted the lid. Inside, there was no gold. There was only a single, tarnished silver coin and a note.

*“You were warned,”* it said.
